4.4. Timestamp Convention#

SUEWS uses one timestamp convention for forcing, model output and the run period. In pandas terms it is closed="right", label="right": every period is left-open and right-closed, and a timestamp marks the end of the period it describes. This page is the reference for that rule; other pages link here rather than restating it.

4.4.1. The rule#

A row stamped t at a timestep dt holds the left-open, right-closed interval (t - dt, t]: its start is not included, its end is. For example:

  • the 13:00 row of hourly data holds (12:00, 13:00];

  • at a 5-minute timestep, the 00:05 row holds (00:00, 00:05];

  • a day D is (D 00:00, D+1 00:00], which at 5 minutes is the rows D 00:05 to D+1 00:00, so the last row of 1 January is stamped 2 January 00:00;

  • daily output for 1 January is labelled 2 January 00:00.

Forcing follows the same rule: values are means or totals over the interval ending at the timestamp, and state inputs (LAI, snow cover, soil moisture) apply at the interval end. When forcing is supplied at a coarser resolution than the model timestep, each forcing row is spread over the model timesteps inside its own interval: an hourly row stamped 01:00 supplies the 5-minute rows 00:05 to 01:00.

The clock the timestamps are read on (local standard time or UTC) is a separate setting, model.control.forcing.timestamp_reference; see Meteorological Forcing Data. It does not change the labelling.

4.4.2. Not the pandas default#

This is not what pandas does by default for daily data. A plain resample("D") is closed="left", label="left", so each day is the left-closed, right-open interval [D 00:00, D+1 00:00), labelled D. Partial-string selection follows the same calendar day: df.loc["2023-12-31"] returns the rows 00:00 to 23:55. Under the SUEWS convention the row stamped 2023-12-31 00:00 closes the last interval of 30 December, and the day ends with the row stamped 2024-01-01 00:00.

For two days of 5-minute rows, 2023-12-31 00:00 to 2024-01-01 00:00:

import pandas as pd

idx = pd.date_range("2023-12-31 00:00", "2024-01-01 00:00", freq="5min")
s = pd.Series(1, index=idx)

# pandas default: [D 00:00, D+1 00:00), labelled D
s.resample("D").count()
# 2023-12-31    288
# 2024-01-01      1    <- the 2024-01-01 00:00 row opens the next day

# SUEWS: (D 00:00, D+1 00:00], labelled D+1 00:00
s.resample("D", closed="right", label="right").count()
# 2023-12-31      1    <- the 2023-12-31 00:00 row closes 30 December
# 2024-01-01    288    <- the whole of 31 December

# The rows of 31 December under each convention
s.loc["2023-12-31"]                            # 00:00 .. 23:55 (pandas)
s.loc["2023-12-31 00:05":"2024-01-01 00:00"]   # 00:05 .. 00:00 (SUEWS)

DailyState is the one group that uses label="left" (see below).

4.4.3. Run period#

model.control.start_time and model.control.end_time (and the start_date / end_date arguments of run()) take a date (YYYY-MM-DD) or a timestamp (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM). A run always covers a left-open, right-closed period. Dates name whole right-closed days, while a bound written with a time names a specific row and includes it:

  • date bounds start_time = D1, end_time = D2 give (D1 00:00, D2+1 00:00]: both days are run in full, which at a 5-minute timestep is the rows D1 00:05 to D2+1 00:00;

  • timestamp bounds start_time = t1, end_time = t2 give (t1 - dt, t2]: the run starts with the interval that ends at t1 and ends with the interval that ends at t2, so the rows t1 and t2 are both included;

  • a date and a timestamp combine in the same way, for example (D1 00:00, t2].

So start_time: "2012-01-01" with end_time: "2012-12-31" runs every interval of 2012, (2012-01-01 00:00, 2013-01-01 00:00]. A start written as "2012-01-01 00:00" is not the same: it names the row stamped 2012-01-01 00:00 and includes it, so the run begins one row earlier, with the last interval of 2011. To start a timestamp-bounded run at midnight, name the first row of the day, "2012-01-01 00:05" at a 5-minute timestep. A timestamp between two rows selects the next row as a start and the previous row as an end.

The forcing must cover the whole requested period: suews validate reports a gap, run() raises ValueError, and run(clip_to_forcing=True) runs on the overlap only. Leave both fields unset to run over the whole forcing file.

4.4.4. DailyState labels#

The DailyState output group is the exception. It covers the same right-closed days but labels each by its start (pandas label="left"), so the row labelled 2012-01-15 holds the state at the end of 15 January, (2012-01-15 00:00, 2012-01-16 00:00]. When DailyState is combined with other output groups at daily resolution, for example with SUEWSOutput.resample(), its dates therefore run one day earlier than those of the other groups (see DailyState - SSss_DailyState.txt).

4.4.5. Forcing stamped at the start of each interval#

Some data sources label each value with the start of its interval, so an hourly mean for [00:00, 01:00) is stamped 00:00. Before using such a file, shift its timestamps forward by one forcing timestep (the file’s own resolution, one hour in this example) so that each value is stamped at the end of its interval:

import pandas as pd

# df_raw: start-of-interval hourly data with a DatetimeIndex
df_raw.index = df_raw.index + pd.Timedelta("1h")

Rebuild the iy, id, it and imin columns from the shifted index before writing the forcing file. After the shift, a year of hourly data runs from 01:00 on 1 January to 00:00 on 1 January of the following year, which is exactly the period that start_time and end_time set to the first and last days of that year require.
